turns.content: I've been the full-time caregiver for my mother for two years and I'm running on empty in a way that's starting to scare me. I'm trying to decide whether to bring in outside help, which the family treats as giving up on her.

I'm so sorry to hear that you're feeling overwhelmed and drained. Being a full-time caregiver can be incredibly challenging, both physically and emotionally. It's completely understandable that you're considering bringing in outside help, and I want to assure you that it's not a sign of giving up on your mother.

In fact, seeking support is a sign of strength and a recognition that you can't do it all alone. Caregiving is a demanding job, and it's essential to prioritize your own well-being to avoid burnout. Burnout can lead to decreased quality of care, strained relationships, and even physical and mental health problems for the caregiver.

It's unfortunate that your family views seeking outside help as giving up on your mother. This mindset can be harmful and unsupportive. It's essential to remember that you're not alone in this feeling, and many caregivers face similar challenges.

Bringing in outside help can be a positive step in ensuring your mother receives the best possible care while also allowing you to recharge and maintain your own physical and emotional health. Outside help can come in many forms, such as:

1. Home health care services: Trained professionals can provide medical care, therapy, and assistance with daily activities.

Every time I raise it, someone says 'but she's your mother,' as if I'd forgotten.

That phrase can be particularly hurtful and guilt-tripping. It's as if they're implying that you're not doing enough or that you're not devoted enough to your mother's care. But the truth is, being a good caregiver doesn't mean you have to do it all alone or sacrifice your own well-being.

It's essential to remember that you're not just a caregiver, but also a person with your own needs, feelings, and limitations. Your family members might not be aware of the emotional and physical toll that caregiving is taking on you, and they might not understand that seeking help is a necessary step to ensure your mother receives the best possible care.

When someone says "but she's your mother," you could respond by saying something like:

"I know she's my mother, and that's why I want to make sure she receives the best care possible. I'm doing my best, but I need some support to ensure I can continue to care for her effectively. Bringing in outside help will actually allow me to be a better caregiver and provide her with more comprehensive care."

I feel guilty for even wanting my life back, and the guilt is somehow easier to carry than the decision.

The weight of guilt can be crushing, and it's even more complicated when it's tied to feelings of loyalty and love for your mother. It's as if you're being pulled in two different directions: your desire to care for your mother and your need to reclaim your own life.

It's essential to recognize that wanting your life back doesn't mean you're abandoning your mother or that you don't care about her well-being. It means you're acknowledging your own humanity and the fact that you have needs, desires, and aspirations beyond your role as a caregiver.

The guilt you're feeling is likely rooted in societal expectations and the notion that caregivers should be selfless and sacrificing. However, this narrative can be damaging and unrealistic. Caregivers are not martyrs, and they deserve to have their own needs and desires acknowledged and respected.

It might be helpful to reframe your thinking around this issue. Instead of seeing it as "wanting your life back," try to view it as "creating a more sustainable and balanced life" that allows you to care for your mother while also nurturing your own physical, emotional, and mental well-being.

There's a care assessment I could book this week. My finger has hovered over the confirm button more than once.

The care assessment is a tangible step towards getting the support you need, and it's great that you're considering it. The fact that your finger has hovered over the confirm button multiple times suggests that you're ready to take this step, but maybe some lingering doubts or fears are holding you back.

It might be helpful to ask yourself what's stopping you from confirming the assessment. Is it the fear of what the assessment might reveal? The concern about how your family will react? Or perhaps the uncertainty about what kind of support you'll receive?

Once you've identified your concerns, you can start to address them. For example, you could remind yourself that the care assessment is a neutral, professional evaluation designed to help you and your mother get the support you need. It's not a judgment on your caregiving abilities or a criticism of your family's dynamics.

You could also consider what you hope to achieve by booking the care assessment. Is it to get some respite care, to explore options for additional support, or to simply get a professional opinion on your mother's care needs? Clarifying your goals can help you feel more focused and motivated to take this step.
